newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. brokers returning to Canadian stock market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. brokers returning to Canadian stock market.

text.p: After an exodus in the late 1980s, U.S. brokers are being lured back to the Canadian market, attracted by Canada's bright economic outlook and booming equities.
Some analysts believe it is just the start of a resurgence of U.S. interest in Canadian equities.

"More and more, the border, at least for financial transactions, seems to be disappearing. And they want to come up here and compete," said Fred Ketchen, director of equity trading at Toronto-based brokerage ScotiaMcLeod Inc.
"I would guess we are going to see five or six renewed, actively trading U.S. houses up here before long. I think that they see the opportunities here," he added.

Merrill Lynch and Co Inc. is the latest U.S. broker to launch a trading operation dedicated to Canadian equities. Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and Morgan Stanley Group Inc. last year expanded their Canadian trading operations.
Privately held Goldman, Sachs has set up a 10-person desk in New York dedicated to Canadian stocks.
"From the equities trading side, we did close down in 1989 and 1990. We are just starting to come back right now," Merrill Lynch Canada chairman Robert Grandy said in a phone interview.
Grandy said many of Merrill's U.S. institutional clients had expressed interest in buying Canadian stocks.
He attributed that to the health of the Canadian economy and relatively lofty U.S. stock markets, which have sent institutions casting about for markets that still have upward potential.
The five-person Merrill operation will be confined to New York for the moment, but Grandy said the company could consider expanding its staff or moving north of the border if business demanded it.
"(We set up this desk) because we are very bullish on Canada. We see growth and opportunities in Canada," said a source at Goldman, who declined to be identified.
The source said Goldman hoped to gain membership of the Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's biggest equities market, by Feb. 1.
Many U.S. brokers, who piled into the Canadian market during the bull market that preceded the 1987 stock market crash, pulled out or cut their involvement in the late 1980s.
In the years after the crash, Toronto stocks failed to matchthe recovery of the New York Stock Exchange, while trading volume and value, the lifeblood of broker profits, dried up.

Last year, the value of stocks changing hands in Toronto reached a record C$301.3 billion ($225 billion). In 1987, total value was just C$100.2 billion ($74.7 billion) and that fell to C$83.5 billion ($62.3 billion) in 1989 and to C$64 billion ($47.7 billion) in 1990.

"We, for a period of time, had lots of U.S. dealers up here, including Merrill Lynch, (Prudential) Bache and some of those. And all of a sudden they all turned around and went back home again," ScotiaMcLeod's Ketchen noted.
But last year foreigners fell in love again with Canadian equity markets.
In 1996, Toronto's key 300 Composite Index rose 25.74 percent, more than double the 11.86 percent gain in 1995. The market is up 2.2 percent so far this year.
